text:
**Short answer:** A pellet smoker draws very little once it's lit, so a roughly 1 kWh power station is enough for an overnight cook. I'd pick the **BLUETTI AC180 (1,152 Wh, $449)**. If you want extra margin for a campsite, I'd pick the **BLUETTI Elite 200 V2**.

**Why a 1 kWh unit is enough**
- A pellet grill has a short igniter burst, then a small steady draw. [Volt & Valley](https://voltandvalley.com/tailgate-travel/best-power-station-for-a-pellet-grill) puts the igniter at about 200–500 W, and says a 1,024 Wh unit covers a full overnight cook at a 40–60 W steady draw.
- A measured example: a Z Grills pellet grill on a Jackery Explorer 1000 used about 194 W at start-up and 35 W while cooking. It used 210 Wh over 6 hours ([Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/power-station-to-run-a-pellet-smoker-overnight), citing RVelectricity).
- Dealectric estimates a 12-hour overnight cook at about 450–750 Wh, including the station's own inverter draw. Cold or windy nights push that toward the top of the range.

**My picks**
1. **BLUETTI AC180, $449 (1,152 Wh).** It covers one night with room to spare. [Buy link](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac180). Dealectric says it's back in stock in late November, so it may not be available right now.
2. **BLUETTI Elite 200 V2, $899 (2,073.6 Wh, 2,600 W inverter).** It covers two or three cooks, which suits a multi-night campsite trip or running phones and lights alongside the smoker. Dealectric lists a code that takes $44.95 off, pre-applied through [this link](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-elite-200-v2). Dealectric is the retailer behind both links, so treat the "tested" code claim as theirs.

**Cheaper or smaller options**
- A 288 Wh unit gives about five hours of cooking. Its surge rating matters more than its capacity: [Volt & Valley](https://voltandvalley.com/tailgate-travel/best-power-station-for-a-pellet-grill) says a 300 W inverter with a 600 W surge is marginal against an igniter that draws 350–500 W.
- The [Grilla Power Station](https://www.grillagrills.com/product/1197809) ($359.99) is sold for pellet grills. It's listed at 300 W output and a 10-hour run time. It's the same marginal 300 W class, so check your grill's igniter wattage first.

**Caveats**
- Check your grill's data plate for igniter wattage. Make sure the station's surge rating clears it.
- Bluetti's own guide ([BLUETTI](https://www.bluettipower.com/blogs/buying-guide/how-long-can-bluetti-power-pellet-grill-smoker)) assumes a higher average draw of 150–250 W. If your grill pulls that much, a 1 kWh unit won't last the night. Test with a watt meter before you rely on it.
- Don't size for an *electric* smoker. Those draw about 1,000 W, and [Home Power Facts](https://homepowerfacts.com/can-it-run/electric-smoker/) found none of the 34 stations it tracks lasts 8 hours on one charge. Pellet smokers are a very different load.
- Keep the battery dry and clear of heat, grease and ash ([GearBrain video summary](https://open.video/%40gearbrain/v/can-a-portable-power-station-run-a-pellet-grill)). Run a full startup-to-shutdown test before the trip.
